catalog_quote: § 5. Accent. Siuslaw exhibits a stress accent, represented here by the acute mark ('); and a pitch accent, designated by the mark (^). Only a limited number of enclitic and proclitic particles show no accent whatsoever. The pitch accent occurs mostly in monosyllabic words that have a short vowel, and lends to the syllable a sharp, abrupt intonation. Both accents are freely shifted from one syllable to another. It seems, however, to be a fixed rule that in the past tense the accent is placed on the first syllable, and that the locative case-endings and the adverbial suffixes must be accented. ... § 12. Effects of Accent. Besides the frequent tendency to lengthen the vowel of the syllable on which it falls, or to lend to it a clear quality, the loss of accent shortens or obscures the quantity of the stem-vowel as soon as it is shifted to one of the suffixed syllables. audit.reasoning: Quote check: both §5 (p. 447) and §12 (pp. 452-453) passages are present verbatim (modulo scanned spacing/ligature slips already normalized) in the held archive.org scanned of HAIL Part 2. Deciding source is the 1922 Boasian reference grammar by the fieldworker himself, the only grammar of this dormant isolate; the set by morphology coding follows directly from Frachtenberg's text (accent not fixed to a syllable; stated regularities are all morphological: past tense initial, locative/adverbial/verbalizing suffixes attract accent, stem vowel reduces when accent shifts to suffix). The only better-informed candidate is Hymes 1966 (15 pp., IJAL, paywalled; archive.org microfilm copy access-restricted), a philological re-analysis rather than new primary data on stress placement, so it is unlikely to overturn the classification but could refine the 'pitch accent' note; hence one medium-priority works still to obtain. Glo
